q: In Rutherford's experiment, most of the alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil passed straight through it. This showed that:
o: The atom's positive charge is spread evenly through it
Most of the atom is empty space
x: If most alpha particles meet nothing that deflects them, the atom must be mostly empty space. The few large-angle deflections were what showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus; an evenly spread positive charge could not produce them.

q: In Rutherford's scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles were turned back through angles greater than 90°. This showed that:
o: The positive charge and almost all the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
Electrons are much heavier than alpha particles
The atom is mostly empty space
Alpha particles are attracted by gold atoms
x: Only a very strong repulsion from a small, massive, positive centre can turn a fast, heavy alpha particle back; the rarity of such events shows the nucleus is tiny. 'Mostly empty space' comes from the particles that went straight through, not from the back-scattered ones.

q: The diameter of an atom is of the order of 10⁻¹⁰ m and that of its nucleus is of the order of 10⁻¹⁴ m. The atom is larger than its nucleus by a factor of about:
x: 10⁻¹⁰ / 10⁻¹⁴ = 10⁴, so the atom is about ten thousand times wider than its nucleus. Multiplying the powers gives 10⁻²⁴, and the reciprocal 10⁻⁴ compares the wrong way round.

q: Tritium, ³₁H, is an isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus contains:
x: Z = 1 gives 1 proton, and A − Z = 3 − 1 = 2 neutrons. Taking A as the number of neutrons gives 3 neutrons; every isotope of hydrogen has exactly 1 proton.

q: An element has two isotopes of mass 10 u and 11 u. A mass spectrograph shows that its average atomic mass is 10.8 u. The percentage of the heavier isotope in the element is:
x: If x is the fraction of the heavier isotope: 11x + 10(1 − x) = 10.8, so x = 0.8 = 80%. Check: 0.8 × 11 + 0.2 × 10 = 8.8 + 2 = 10.8 u. Giving the fraction to the lighter isotope gives 20%.

q: The binding energy of a nucleus is the energy:
o: Needed to remove one electron from the atom
Released when the nucleus emits an alpha particle
Needed to separate the nucleus completely into its free protons and neutrons
Of the electrons orbiting the nucleus
x: Binding energy is the work needed to pull all the nucleons apart; equally, it is the energy released when the nucleus forms from free nucleons, and it equals the mass defect × c². Removing an electron is ionisation, an atomic (not nuclear) process.

q: Energy is released both when very light nuclei fuse and when very heavy nuclei split. This is because in both processes:
o: The binding energy per nucleon of the products is greater than that of the reactants
The total number of nucleons increases
The binding energy per nucleon of the products is smaller
x: The binding-energy-per-nucleon curve peaks near iron-56. Fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both move towards the peak, so the products are more tightly bound and the extra binding energy is released, with a matching loss of mass. Nucleon number is conserved.

q: Taking 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, the energy equivalent of 1 u of mass is about:
x: E = mc² = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ × 9 × 10¹⁶ ≈ 1.49 × 10⁻¹⁰ J, and 1.49 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ ≈ 930 MeV, the familiar 1 u = 931 MeV. Dividing by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ (the eV) and calling the result MeV gives 9.3 × 10⁸ MeV; a slip of 10³ gives 0.93 MeV.

q: On the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, for nuclei heavier than iron-56 the binding energy per nucleon:
o: Increases steadily as the mass number increases
Decreases slowly as the mass number increases
Is the same for every nucleus
x: After its peak of about 8.8 MeV near iron-56, the curve falls slowly, to about 7.6 MeV for uranium-238, because the growing proton-proton repulsion makes large nuclei less tightly bound. A steady rise describes only the light nuclei.

q: The binding energy of carbon-12 is 92.2 MeV and that of carbon-13 is 97.1 MeV. The energy needed to remove one neutron from a carbon-13 nucleus, leaving carbon-12, is:
x: Removing the neutron leaves a carbon-12 nucleus plus a free neutron, so the energy needed is the difference in binding energies: 97.1 − 92.2 = 4.9 MeV. 7.5 MeV and 7.7 MeV are the average binding energies per nucleon (97.1/13 and 92.2/12), not the energy for this neutron; adding gives 189.3 MeV.

q: A nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U emits one alpha particle and then two beta (β⁻) particles one after the other. The final nucleus is:
x: The alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th (A − 4, Z − 2); each β⁻ raises Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged, so Z goes 90 → 92 and the product is ²³⁴₉₂U, an isotope of the parent. Stopping after the alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th; taking 4 more off A for the beta decays gives ²³⁰₉₂U, and raising Z by 2 for each β⁻ gives Z = 94.

q: The radioactive series that starts with ²³²₉₀Th ends with the stable nucleus ²⁰⁸₈₂Pb. The numbers of alpha and beta (β⁻) particles emitted in the whole series are:
x: Only alpha decay changes A: (232 − 208)/4 = 6 alpha particles. These lower Z by 12, to 78, but the final Z is 82, so 82 − 78 = 4 β⁻ decays raised it. Taking the drop in Z (8) as the number of beta decays gives 6 alpha and 8 beta.

q: A radioactive sample is left for a time equal to three of its half-lives. The fraction of the original nuclei that have decayed is:
x: After 3 half-lives the fraction left is (½)³ = 1/8, so the fraction decayed is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. Giving the fraction remaining (1/8) instead of the fraction decayed is the usual slip.

q: A sample contains 5 × 10¹⁵ radioactive nuclei of a nuclide with half-life 693 s. Using λ = 0.693/T½, the activity of the sample is:
x: λ = 0.693/693 = 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹, so A = λN = 10⁻³ × 5 × 10¹⁵ = 5 × 10¹² Bq. Dividing N by T½ without the 0.693 gives 7.2 × 10¹² Bq; multiplying N by 0.693 alone gives 3.5 × 10¹⁵ Bq.

q: The SI unit of the activity of a radioactive source, the becquerel (Bq), is equal to:
o: The activity of 1 g of radium
x: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second. One joule per kilogram is the gray (absorbed dose), and the activity of 1 g of radium is the old unit, the curie.

q: A Geiger-Müller tube detects radiation because the radiation:
o: Makes the gas glow so brightly that it is seen
Ionises the low-pressure gas in the tube, starting an avalanche of ions that gives a pulse of current
Heats the central wire until it melts
Condenses vapour into droplets along its path
x: An entering particle ionises the gas; the high voltage accelerates the freed electrons, which ionise more atoms (an avalanche), and the resulting pulse is counted. Droplets along the path are how a cloud chamber shows tracks.

q: In a solid-state (semiconductor) detector, radiation is detected when it enters a reverse-biased p-n junction and:
o: Makes the junction forward biased permanently
Produces electron-hole pairs, which give a small pulse of current
x: Radiation passing through the depletion region creates electron-hole pairs; the reverse-bias field sweeps them out as a pulse of current, whose size depends on the energy deposited. Visible droplet tracks belong to a cloud chamber.

q: A tissue receives an absorbed dose of 0.01 Gy of alpha radiation, whose quality factor (RBE) is 20. The equivalent dose is:
x: Equivalent dose = absorbed dose × quality factor = 0.01 × 20 = 0.2 Sv. Alpha particles do much more biological damage per joule than gamma rays, which have factor 1. Dividing by 20 gives 0.0005 Sv; ignoring the factor gives 0.01 Sv.

q: The dose rate from a small gamma-ray source is 8 μGy per hour at a distance of 1 m. Ignoring absorption in air, the dose rate at 2 m from the source is:
x: Radiation from a point source spreads over a sphere, so intensity ∝ 1/r²: doubling the distance divides the dose rate by 4, giving 8/4 = 2 μGy per hour. Treating it as ∝ 1/r gives 4 μGy per hour. This is why keeping a distance is a key safety rule.

q: A GM counter placed near a radioactive source shows 50 counts per minute; with the source removed it shows a background of 10 counts per minute. With the source back in the same place, the reading after two half-lives of the source will be:
x: The source alone gives 50 − 10 = 40 counts per minute, which falls to 40/4 = 10 after two half-lives; adding the unchanged background gives 10 + 10 = 20 counts per minute. Halving the total reading twice (50/4) gives 12.5; forgetting the background gives 10.

q: In a nuclear power reactor, the coolant (such as water or carbon dioxide gas) is used to:
o: Absorb neutrons so that the chain reaction stops
Carry the heat from the reactor core to the heat exchanger, where steam is made
x: The coolant removes the heat produced by fission in the core and carries it to the heat exchanger, where it turns water into steam for the turbines. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods, and slowing them is the moderator's job.

q: A piece of uranium-235 smaller than the critical mass cannot sustain a chain reaction because:
o: Too many of the neutrons released escape from its surface before causing further fissions
Its nuclei cannot undergo fission at all
It releases no neutrons when it undergoes fission
x: In a small piece the surface is large compared with the volume, so many neutrons escape and, on average, fewer than one neutron per fission causes another fission. Each fission still releases 2-3 neutrons; the problem is losing them.

q: A fission of U-235 (236 nucleons in all, with the neutron) releases about 200 MeV. A fusion of deuterium and tritium (5 nucleons in all) releases about 17.6 MeV. Per nucleon taking part, which releases more energy, and by roughly how much?
o: Both release the same per nucleon
x: Fusion: 17.6/5 ≈ 3.5 MeV per nucleon; fission: 200/236 ≈ 0.85 MeV per nucleon, so fusion gives about 4 times as much per nucleon. Comparing energy per reaction (200/17.6 ≈ 11) instead of per nucleon makes fission look larger.

q: Natural uranium contains only about 0.7% of the fissile isotope U-235, the rest being mostly U-238. Many power reactors use enriched uranium, which means uranium in which:
o: The percentage of U-235 has been increased
The percentage of U-238 has been increased
Extra neutrons have been added to each nucleus
The uranium has been turned into plutonium
x: Slow neutrons cause fission mainly in U-235, so raising its share (to a few per cent) makes a chain reaction easier to sustain. Neutrons cannot simply be added to nuclei, and enrichment does not change uranium into another element.
